summary: A Network Host Status report covering July 31 to August 4, 1972. It lists the terminal IMPs and hosts that were left out of daily testing because they were intended only as users.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reports status information for network hosts over five days. It explains how the tests were labeled and announces that this series of summaries will stop.

questions: which arpanet hosts were up in 1972
which arpanet hosts were available in august 1972
what do the host status codes mean
subtitle: A weekly table of ARPANET host reachability tests and status reports.

tldr.problem: Network users needed information about which hosts were available and accepting connections.
tldr.mechanism: BBN reports host status from July 31 through August 4 and defines the letters used in its test table.
tldr.outcome: The RFC announces that these summaries will stop and notes that other survey information may be available.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 376 as Unknown and says it updates RFC 370. The RFC states that publication of these summaries will be discontinued.

sections.title: Hosts Included in the Report
sections.content:
The report covers most network hosts from July 31 to August 4. Some hosts are excluded from daily tests because they are intended to be users only, including listed Terminal IMPs and the Network Control Center computer used to gather statistics.

The tables list host addresses, sites, computers, reported status or prediction, and the source of that information.
sections.plainLanguage: The report covers hosts tested during the stated period. It leaves out some machines used only to access the network or gather statistics.

sections.title: Status and Prediction Table
sections.content:
The first table gives a status or prediction for each listed host, such as Server, User Only, Soon, Never or a limited service. It also identifies the person who supplied the information.

The report explains that the UCLA IBM-360/91 offered NETRJS, which the BBN Terminal IMP could not test. For that host, the report assumes that a connection to the NETRJS logger indicates the service works.
sections.plainLanguage: The table combines reported service information with an estimate of whether a host is available. Some entries are not direct results of the daily connection test.

sections.title: Daily Test Results
sections.content:
The second table shows a result for each tested host on five dates. Open means the host opened a connection and was accessible; half open means it opened and then closed or stopped responding; full means it reported all network ports in use; refused means it returned CLS; timed out means no ICP and connection completed within 60 seconds; dead means the host was inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.

A hash marks sites that said their systems might not be available at those times.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test result has a letter that describes what happened during connection setup. For example, Open means a host accepted the connection, while Timed out means setup did not finish within 60 seconds.

sections.title: End of This Series
sections.content: The note says Ellen Westheimer left BBN on August 4 and that publication of these summaries would therefore stop. Alex McKenzie says UCLA-NMC was considering similar, more detailed survey data and points to online survey information at MIT-DMCG in RFC 308.
sections.plainLanguage: The author says the summaries will stop after the person preparing them leaves BBN. The note points to other host-survey information.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

items.label: Half open
items.desc: Host opened a connection but closed it or stopped responding.

items.label: Full
items.desc: Host said all network ports were in use and closed the connection.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: Host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: ICP and connection were not completed within 60 seconds.

items.label: Dead
items.desc: Host was dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.

references.text: RFC 370, an earlier Network Host Status report.
RFC 308, on online survey information at MIT-DMCG.
